laws.title: Egyptian Culture — Hospitality and Islamic Customs
laws.subtitle: Tea and food always accepted; dress modestly
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's hospitality is legendary — accept offered tea and food always. Islamic customs: right hand for giving and receiving, dress modestly (especially women). Greetings among men: handshake, sometimes followed by touching cheeks. 'Ahlan wa sahlan' (welcome) is a common greeting. During Ramadan, be discreet about eating and drinking in public.
laws.penalty: Disrespecting religious customs or Islamic law: possible legal consequences in extreme cases.
exceptions: Beach resorts and tourist areas have more relaxed dress codes
Cairo is more cosmopolitan than rural areas

quiz.q: What should you always do when offered tea in Egypt?
quiz.explanation: Accepting offered tea in Egypt is a sign of respect for hospitality — refusing is considered impolite.

laws.title: Pyramid & Heritage Site Rules — Climbing the Pyramids is Illegal
laws.subtitle: Antiquities Law — Climbing or damaging monuments: imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Climbing the Pyramids of Giza is illegal and carries a prison sentence. In 2023, a Danish tourist was fined and briefly detained for climbing. Photography inside certain tombs requires special paid permits, and flash photography is generally banned (damages ancient pigments). Removing any soil, stone, or artefact from any archaeological site is a serious criminal offence under Egypt's Antiquities Law.
laws.penalty: Climbing pyramids: fine + possible imprisonment. Removing artefacts: up to 25 years imprisonment. Unpermitted photography in tombs: fine.
exceptions: Official licensed tours with photography permits
Academic archaeological expeditions with government permits

quiz.q: Is climbing the Pyramids of Giza legal?
options: No — it is illegal and carries a fine or imprisonment
quiz.explanation: Climbing Egypt's Pyramids is illegal — in 2023, a tourist was detained and fined for doing so.

laws.title: Photography Restrictions — Military, Police and Bridges
laws.subtitle: Law 313/1954 — Photographing officials or military is forbidden
laws.fullDescription: In Egypt, photographing police officers, soldiers, government buildings, bridges, ports, airports infrastructure, and railway stations can lead to arrest. The law is broad and inconsistently applied — tourists have been detained for photographing what seemed like ordinary streets that included a police presence. Drone photography requires advance permits and is banned near antiquities sites and the Nile.
laws.penalty: Photographing prohibited areas: detention, camera confiscation, criminal charges. Serious cases: imprisonment.
exceptions: Tourist sites and open-air monuments in daylight
Advance permit for legitimate commercial photography

quiz.q: What can happen if you photograph a police officer in Egypt?
quiz.explanation: Egyptian Law 313/1954 prohibits photographing police, military, and government infrastructure — tourists have been arrested for doing so.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Laws — Criminal Under Debauchery Laws
laws.subtitle: Penal Code Art. 9 — Up to 3 years for 'debauchery'
laws.fullDescription: Egypt criminalises same-sex relations under vague 'debauchery' laws (Article 9 of Law 10/1961) rather than an explicit sodomy law. This gives authorities broad discretion — people have been arrested from dating apps (Grindr raids are documented), at private parties, and even at a concert for raising a rainbow flag. In 2017, police arrested 57 people after a rainbow flag was raised at a Mashrou' Leila concert. Egypt has become increasingly hostile to LGBTQ+ people in recent years, with social media used as evidence in prosecutions.
laws.penalty: 'Debauchery': up to 3 years imprisonment. 'Habitual debauchery': up to 5 years. Police entrapment via apps is documented.
exceptions: No legal exceptions — private conduct is also prosecutable
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Penal Code — Law 10/1961 on Combating Prostitution

quiz.q: How do Egyptian authorities typically prosecute same-sex relations?
options: Under vague 'debauchery' laws, including through dating app stings
quiz.explanation: Egypt uses vague 'debauchery' laws (not explicit sodomy laws) to prosecute LGBTQ+ people — documented tactics include Grindr stings, rainbow flag arrests, and raids on private parties.

laws.title: Photography Restrictions — Military Sites and Government Buildings
laws.subtitle: Law No. 97 of 1992 — Photographing prohibited areas
laws.fullDescription: Photographing military installations, police stations, government buildings, bridges, canals, and certain public infrastructure is strictly prohibited in Egypt. Egypt is highly security-conscious, especially since 2011. Tourists have been arrested and had their equipment confiscated for photographing seemingly innocuous targets near restricted areas. The Suez Canal is a particularly sensitive zone. Photography of poverty, street begging, and 'unflattering' images of Egyptian life has also caused problems with police.
laws.penalty: Photographing restricted sites: arrest, confiscation of equipment, and prosecution under security laws — fines and up to 1 year imprisonment. Military photography: more severe charges possible.
exceptions: Tourist sites like the Pyramids, Luxor, and Karnak have designated photography areas
All photography: ask for permission when in doubt, especially near official buildings

quiz.q: What types of locations are illegal to photograph in Egypt?
options: Military installations, police stations, bridges, and government buildings
quiz.explanation: Egypt prohibits photography of military installations, police stations, bridges, and government buildings — tourists have been arrested for what seemed like innocent shots near restricted zones.

laws.title: Antiquities Export Ban — Even a Pottery Shard Can Land You in Prison
laws.subtitle: Law No. 117 of 1983 (Antiquities Protection Law) — All ancient artefacts are state property
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Antiquities Protection Law (Law No. 117 of 1983, amended by Law No. 3 of 2010) declares all archaeological artefacts found on Egyptian soil to be the property of the Egyptian state — regardless of how they were obtained. Removing any antiquity from Egypt without an official export permit from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities is a serious criminal offence. This applies not just to statues and jewellery but to pottery shards, coins, inscribed stones, mummies or mummy parts, and even fragments collected from the surface at archaeological sites. Tourists have been arrested at Cairo International Airport attempting to leave with items bought at informal markets that turned out to be genuine artefacts. Customs screening is thorough, and specialist antiquities police operate at airports and ports. Egypt has also aggressively pursued repatriation claims internationally, recovering major pieces from museums and private collections abroad.
laws.penalty: Smuggling or attempting to export antiquities: imprisonment of 3 to 15 years and heavy fines. Items seized and confiscated. Egyptian authorities may pursue charges even after the traveller returns home via international legal channels.
exceptions: Licensed dealers may sell modern reproductions with a certificate of authenticity confirming the item is not a genuine antiquity
Officially approved museum loans and academic research transfers require Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities permits
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Law No. 117 of 1983 — Antiquities Protection Law

quiz.q: Under Egyptian law, who owns archaeological artefacts found on Egyptian soil?
options: The landowner on whose property they were found
The finder, under a 50/50 sharing rule with the state
The Egyptian state — all artefacts are state property regardless of origin
quiz.explanation: Egyptian Law No. 117 of 1983 declares all antiquities found on Egyptian soil to be the property of the Egyptian state. Taking even a pottery shard out of the country without a permit is a criminal offence carrying up to 15 years in prison.

laws.title: Antiquities Export Ban — All Pharaonic Artefacts State Property
laws.subtitle: Law 117/1983 (Protection of Antiquities) — 15 years to life + heavy fines
laws.fullDescription: Since 1983, all Egyptian antiquities — every object over 100 years old that is of historical or artistic significance — are declared state property under Law 117/1983, as amended. Export of antiquities is almost entirely prohibited; private possession is permitted only if registered with the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities before 1983. Souvenir shops openly sell ‘antique-looking’ items that are either fakes or smuggled; either way carrying them through Cairo International Airport is risky. X-ray scanning at departure is routine. In 2018 a German tourist was sentenced to five years for attempting to export a small stone statue he had bought at a market. Archaeological excavations are tightly controlled; the Supreme Council of Antiquities must authorise all digs, and findings remain in Egypt. Coral and Red Sea shells are also protected under environmental law and cannot be exported.
laws.penalty: Smuggling of antiquities out of Egypt: 15 years to life imprisonment + fine up to EGP 1 million under Law 117/1983. Trading without licence: up to 5 years imprisonment. Damaging an antiquity site: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Reproductions bearing a Ministry of Tourism authentication stamp identifying them as modern replicas
Items registered and documented in private collections before the 1983 legislation
laws.sourceLabel: Law 117/1983 (Protection of Antiquities) — Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

quiz.q: Under Egyptian Law 117/1983, what is the status of ancient artefacts found in Egypt?
options: They may be freely exported if purchased
They belong to whoever excavates them
They are state property — export is almost entirely prohibited
Export is allowed with a $100 permit
quiz.explanation: Law 117/1983 declares all antiquities over 100 years old to be state property. Export is almost entirely prohibited; smuggling can result in 15 years to life imprisonment.

laws.title: Red Sea Coral Protection — Touching or Breaking Coral Is a Criminal Offence
laws.subtitle: Egyptian Environmental Law 4/1994 — Coral: up to 5 years + EGP 50,000 fine
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Red Sea coastline hosts some of the world's most diverse and pristine coral reef systems — the Ras Mohammed National Park and the Straits of Tiran are among the finest diving destinations on Earth. Egypt's Environmental Protection Law No. 4/1994 makes it a serious criminal offence to break, remove, or damage coral reefs. Touching coral while diving or snorkelling is illegal, as body oils kill polyps. Using gloves while diving (which can encourage touching) is banned in some Egyptian dive sites. Sunscreen containing oxybenzone is banned in several Red Sea resort areas. Taking shells, coral fragments, or starfish from the beach is also illegal.
laws.penalty: Breaking or removing coral: up to 5 years imprisonment + EGP 50,000 fine. Sunscreen violations: fine. Taking shells: administrative fine + confiscation.
exceptions: Licensed scientific research with Ministry of Environment permit
Emergency anchoring for safety reasons
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency — Marine Protected Areas

quiz.q: Under Egyptian Environmental Law 4/1994, what is the maximum prison sentence for breaking or removing coral from the Red Sea?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's Environmental Protection Law No. 4/1994 imposes up to 5 years imprisonment for breaking, removing, or damaging coral reefs — reflecting the critical ecological importance of the Red Sea's reef systems.

laws.title: Antiquities Export Ban — Severe Penalties for Cultural Artifact Smuggling
laws.subtitle: Removing Egyptian antiquities is illegal and treated as a serious criminal offense
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Law No. 117 of 1983 (Antiquities Protection Law) and its 2010 amendments create one of the world's strictest cultural heritage protection regimes. All objects predating 1882 are considered state property regardless of who possesses them. Purchasing antiquities from unauthorized dealers, even inadvertently, is illegal. Carrying any ancient artifact through customs without official documentation results in immediate arrest. The Egyptian Museum has refused to accept objects from private donors that cannot prove unimpeachable provenance. Egypt has successfully repatriated thousands of pieces from foreign museums. Photography inside certain tombs and burial chambers in the Valley of the Kings requires paid permits.
laws.penalty: Antiquities smuggling: 3–15 years imprisonment + fines equal to 5–10x the estimated market value. Receiving stolen antiquities: 1–7 years + fines. Unauthorized excavation: 7 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Licensed archaeological expeditions with Ministry of Antiquities permits
Diplomatic transfers for official exhibition loans
Objects with documented pre-1882 export records
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities — Heritage Law

quiz.q: Under Egyptian law, objects predating what year are automatically considered state property?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's Law No. 117 of 1983 considers all objects predating 1882 — the year British occupation began — to be state property, regardless of current possession or where they were found.

laws.title: Emergency Law and Mass Surveillance — Egypt's Permanent Security State Since 2017
laws.subtitle: Egypt's state of emergency (2017–2021) and cybercrime law enable broad repression of dissent
laws.fullDescription: Egypt maintained a near-continuous state of emergency from 1967 to 2012, and reimposed it following the 2017 Sinai church bombings — keeping it in force until 2021. President el-Sisi's government has used emergency powers and the 2018 Cybercrime Law to arrest journalists, bloggers, and ordinary citizens. The Law on Combating Information Technology Crimes criminalizes content that 'threatens national security, social peace, or public order.' Websites including Al Jazeera, Mada Masr, and hundreds of others are blocked. Egypt arrested over 60,000 political prisoners between 2013–2020 by estimates. The Supreme State Security Prosecution (SSSP) handles political cases — defendants can be detained for up to 2 years without trial. Egypt is one of the world's top jailers of journalists.
laws.penalty: Cybercrime/social media offenses against state: 1–5 years imprisonment + fines up to EGP 300,000 (~$9,700). Joining banned organizations (Muslim Brotherhood): life imprisonment. Terrorism: death penalty.
exceptions: State-sanctioned media operate freely
Foreign correspondents with MENA accreditation have limited protections
Diplomatic missions can use encrypted communications without restriction
laws.sourceLabel: Human Rights Watch — Egypt World Report 2023

quiz.q: Approximately how many political prisoners did Egypt arrest between 2013 and 2020, according to human rights estimates?
quiz.explanation: Human rights organizations estimate Egypt arrested over 60,000 political prisoners between 2013 (after the military coup removing President Morsi) and 2020 — making Egypt one of the world's leading jailers of political detainees and journalists during this period.

laws.title: Nile Dam Dispute — Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam vs. Egypt's Water Security Laws
laws.subtitle: Egypt views the GERD dam as an existential water threat; negotiations have stalled for a decade
laws.fullDescription: Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) — completed 2023, Africa's largest hydroelectric project — sits on the Blue Nile, which supplies 85% of the Nile's water reaching Egypt. Egypt depends on the Nile for 97% of its freshwater. The 1929 and 1959 Nile Water Agreements gave Egypt 55.5 billion cubic meters per year and a veto over upstream projects — agreements Ethiopia rejects as colonial-era impositions. Negotiations mediated by the African Union, US, and World Bank have repeatedly failed. Egypt's constitution commits the government to 'protect the Nile water rights and not take any act that would harm those rights.' Egypt has not ruled out military action. Sudan's position has shifted — it initially supported GERD for electricity. GERD's first two filling seasons reduced Nile flows to Egypt measurably.
laws.penalty: Domestic violations of Egypt's National Water Resources Plan: administrative fines + criminal prosecution for industrial theft of water. International Nile dispute: diplomatic and potentially military dimensions.
exceptions: Emergency water sharing protocols during severe drought years (under discussion)
Scientific data sharing agreements between riparian states
ICOLD-certified dam safety inspections
laws.sourceLabel: International Water Law Project — Nile Waters Agreements

quiz.q: What percentage of Egypt's freshwater comes from the Nile River?
quiz.explanation: Egypt depends on the Nile for approximately 97% of its freshwater — making any upstream diversion or storage project an existential concern for Egyptian water security. This explains why Egypt views Ethiopia's GERD dam (which can store 74 billion cubic meters, more than Egypt's entire annual allocation) as a potentially catastrophic threat.

laws.title: Currency Crisis & IMF Bailout Cycle
laws.subtitle: Egypt's pound lost 70% of value in two years as $100 billion in debt came due
laws.fullDescription: Egypt under President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi embarked on massive debt-financed construction projects — a new administrative capital, Suez Canal expansion, highways — accumulating over $165 billion in external debt. When global interest rates rose, Egypt faced a crisis: foreign currency reserves depleted, the pound was devalued multiple times (losing ~70% vs the dollar between 2022–2024), and inflation exceeded 38%. Egypt received three IMF programs totaling over $20 billion between 2016 and 2024. A $35 billion UAE investment in Ras El Hekma (February 2024) provided critical relief. Egypt is among the world's most indebted emerging markets.
laws.penalty: Parallel currency market trading (black market): criminal prosecution for unlicensed exchange dealers. Import restrictions on luxury goods: fines and confiscation. Food subsidy fraud: imprisonment.
exceptions: Tourism dollar earnings are exempt from most import restrictions
Suez Canal revenues remain in foreign currency
Egyptian diaspora remittances (over $28 billion annually) are a key foreign currency source

quiz.q: By approximately how much did Egypt's pound depreciate against the dollar between 2022 and 2024?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's pound lost approximately 70% of its value against the US dollar between 2022 and 2024, driven by external debt pressures, depleted foreign reserves, and a series of forced devaluations required under IMF programs.

laws.title: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Water War
laws.subtitle: Egypt considers the Nile dam an existential threat — water talks collapsed repeatedly since 2011
laws.fullDescription: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile — Africa's largest hydroelectric project, producing 6,000 MW when complete — has created one of the world's most dangerous water disputes. Egypt considers the Nile an existential resource (97% of its freshwater), protected by the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement giving Egypt 55.5 billion cubic meters annually. Ethiopia argues the colonial-era treaty is illegitimate and that GERD is a development right. Ethiopia completed the dam in 2022–2023 and began filling the reservoir. The African Union mediation failed; Egypt threatened military action; a 2024 Egyptian-Ethiopian summit produced marginal progress.
laws.penalty: Egypt's 1959 Nile Waters Agreement claims legal force over all upstream usage. No binding international mechanism exists — only diplomatic pressure. Egypt has stated military options remain on the table.
exceptions: International law of transboundary watercourses (UN Watercourses Convention) requires equitable utilization and no significant harm
Ethiopia has not signed the UN Convention — Egypt has
A tripartite (Egypt-Sudan-Ethiopia) framework is the only multilateral mechanism available
laws.sourceLabel: Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs — GERD

quiz.q: What percentage of Egypt's freshwater comes from the Nile, making the GERD dispute existential?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 97% of Egypt's freshwater comes from the Nile River, making Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam an existential threat in Egyptian strategic thinking — and the basis for Egypt's repeated threats to use military force if necessary to protect its water supply.

laws.title: 2019 Constitutional Amendments: Sisi's Power Extension
laws.subtitle: Egypt amended its constitution to allow Sisi to rule until 2030 and gave the military permanent political oversight
laws.fullDescription: In April 2019, Egypt held a referendum approving constitutional amendments that reset President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's term limits, potentially allowing him to remain in power until 2030 (and beyond with further amendments). The amendments also extended presidential terms from 4 to 6 years, gave the military a formal constitutional role as 'guardian of democracy,' and granted the president power to appoint judges. The referendum was approved by 88.8% of voters — a figure widely questioned by civil society groups who cited mass coercion and lack of genuine campaigning for the 'No' side. Egypt scores near the bottom of global press freedom and human rights indices.
laws.penalty: Publicly opposing the amendments or calling for boycotts: arrest under anti-protest laws. Up to 5 years imprisonment for 'spreading false news' about the referendum
exceptions: A formal 'No' campaign was technically permitted but faced severe practical restrictions
Some Coptic Christian community leaders were seen as supportive of Sisi's extended tenure

quiz.q: Until what year do Egypt's 2019 constitutional amendments potentially allow President Sisi to remain in power?
quiz.explanation: The 2019 amendments reset Sisi's term clock and, combined with the extension of presidential terms to 6 years, create a framework allowing him to remain in power until at least 2030.

laws.title: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam: Egypt's Existential Water Crisis
laws.subtitle: Ethiopia's massive Nile dam threatens Egypt's water supply — a dispute Egypt calls an existential threat and has hinted could justify military action
laws.fullDescription: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile is Africa's largest hydroelectric dam, with a reservoir that can hold more than the annual flow of the entire Nile. Ethiopia began filling it in 2020. Egypt depends on the Nile for 97% of its freshwater and views any reduction in flow as an existential threat. Egypt's official position is that the 1929 and 1959 Nile Water Agreements give Egypt veto rights over upstream dams — agreements Ethiopia refuses to recognize. Egypt has explicitly not ruled out military action. Sudan has alternated between supporting Ethiopia and Egypt. UN Security Council discussions have not produced binding resolutions. The dam is expected to take 4–7 years to fully fill.
laws.penalty: No domestic penalties — this is international law. Egypt's official position threatens legal action at the UN and African Union, and has not excluded military options
exceptions: The AU-mediated negotiations have continued without binding agreement
Sudan's position has complicated what might otherwise be a bilateral dispute

quiz.q: What percentage of Egypt's freshwater comes from the Nile?
quiz.explanation: Egypt depends on the Nile for approximately 97% of its freshwater supply — making it one of the world's most water-dependent nations and explaining why the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is viewed in Cairo as an existential national security threat.

laws.title: Antiquities Export Ban
laws.subtitle: Egypt criminalizes smuggling ancient artifacts — zero tolerance
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Law on the Protection of Antiquities (Law 117/1983, amended 2010) bans the private ownership, sale, or export of any antiquity predating 1952 without explicit government authorization. Smuggling ancient artifacts is a criminal offense punishable by up to 25 years in prison. Egypt has aggressively pursued the return of illegally exported artifacts from international museums and auction houses under UNESCO conventions. Notable recoveries include items from the Louvre, Christie's auctions, and US museums. Since 2021, Egypt has demanded the return of the Rosetta Stone from the British Museum.
laws.penalty: Up to 25 years imprisonment and heavy fines for smuggling or unauthorized sale; confiscation of all artifacts
exceptions: Licensed dealers may sell authenticated modern reproductions
State museums and archaeological missions operate under separate permits
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

quiz.q: What famous artifact has Egypt demanded be returned from the British Museum?
quiz.explanation: Egypt has demanded the return of the Rosetta Stone — discovered in 1799 and taken to Britain — from the British Museum, where it has been since 1802. The UK has so far declined.

laws.title: Nile Water Rights Law
laws.subtitle: Egypt claims historical rights to the Nile under colonial-era treaties
laws.fullDescription: Egypt claims a historical right to approximately 55.5 billion cubic meters of Nile water per year under the disputed 1959 Nile Waters Agreement between Egypt and Sudan (which excluded other Nile basin nations). Egypt has consistently opposed upstream projects — particularly Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) — arguing they violate these historical rights. The dispute has been framed as an existential national security issue in Egypt, where 90% of the population depends on the Nile. Egypt's 2014 Constitution (Article 44) designates Nile water security as a state obligation, and Egyptian law imposes strict criminal penalties on any unauthorized diversion of irrigation water.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized water theft from the Nile or irrigation system: criminal fines and imprisonment; international breaches handled diplomatically
exceptions: The 1959 agreement is disputed by upstream nations who were not parties to it
Sudan and Egypt have different positions on the GERD filling timeline
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation

quiz.q: What is the GERD?
options: Nile Governance Engagement and Resource Deal
quiz.explanation: GERD stands for Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam — the massive hydroelectric dam on the Blue Nile in Ethiopia that has been a source of intense geopolitical conflict between Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan since construction began in 2011.

laws.title: New Administrative Capital Law
laws.subtitle: Egypt built an entirely new capital city under presidential decree
laws.fullDescription: Egypt began building a New Administrative Capital (NAC) in 2015 by presidential decree — a purpose-built city 45km east of Cairo, designed for 6.5 million people and to house all government ministries and eventually Parliament. The project is run by the Administrative Capital for Urban Development (ACUD), a joint venture between the government and the military's engineering arm (AAEC). The capital relocation required constitutional and legal amendments specifying that Cairo would remain Egypt's symbolic capital. By 2024, government ministries had begun moving to the NAC. The project cost is estimated at $58 billion, making it one of the world's largest urban construction projects.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized construction within the NAC boundaries: demolition orders; land speculation in designated zones: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Existing Suez Canal zone cities have separate administrative frameworks
Cairo remains constitutionally Egypt's capital — NAC is the 'new capital' only informally

quiz.q: How far from Cairo is Egypt's New Administrative Capital being built?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's New Administrative Capital is being built approximately 45km east of Cairo in the desert, with plans to house 6.5 million people and serve as the seat of government — one of the world's largest new city-building projects.

laws.title: State of Emergency and Emergency Powers Law
laws.subtitle: Egypt maintained a state of emergency for most of its modern history, normalizing exceptional powers
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Emergency Law (Law No. 162 of 1958) grants the president sweeping powers during a declared state of emergency: suspending constitutional rights, allowing indefinite detention without charge, establishing emergency state security courts with limited appeal rights, restricting movement and assembly, and censoring communications. Egypt was under continuous states of emergency from 1981 (Sadat assassination) until 2012, and again from 2017 (after the Sinai mosque attack) until 2021 — representing 32 of 40 years under emergency law. The 2019 constitutional amendments extended President el-Sisi's term and allowed him to serve until 2030, while also giving the military broad powers to protect 'the state and its civilian government.' Critics note that even after the emergency law lapsed, many of its powers were incorporated into permanent legislation (Counter-terrorism law, Cybercrime law) effectively institutionalizing emergency-era restrictions.
laws.penalty: Emergency courts have prosecuted tens of thousands of political detainees; penalties range from fines to death sentences; emergency court decisions historically had limited appeal rights
exceptions: Diplomatic missions are exempt from emergency search/seizure
Healthcare facilities have operational exemptions
Religious institutions have limited exemption for religious practice

laws.title: Nile Water Rights and Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Dispute
laws.subtitle: Egypt's existential dependence on Nile water creates a major legal conflict with Ethiopia's mega-dam
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's legal and geopolitical conflict with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) — a 6,450 megawatt hydroelectric dam on the Blue Nile — represents one of the most significant transboundary water disputes in the world. Egypt considers the Nile existential: approximately 97% of Egypt's freshwater comes from the Nile, and Egypt's 1959 bilateral agreement with Sudan allocated 55.5 billion cubic meters per year to Egypt and 18.5 billion to Sudan — with no allocation to upstream countries including Ethiopia. Ethiopia argues the 1959 agreement is colonial-era and does not bind it. The GERD's reservoir (Africa's largest) can hold approximately 74 billion cubic meters. Egypt's Constitution (Article 44) declares protection of the Nile 'a national duty' and Egypt has repeatedly threatened military action if filling the dam damages its water supply. The African Union has mediated without agreement.
laws.penalty: Egypt has no direct legal enforcement mechanism over Ethiopia; Egypt's constitution obligates Egyptian officials to protect Nile water rights; Nile basin countries not party to 1959 agreement dispute its binding nature
exceptions: The 2010 Entebbe Agreement (signed by most upstream Nile countries but not Egypt and Sudan) creates a competing legal framework
International Law Commission guidelines on shared watercourses apply without enforcement mechanism
Bilateral military agreements between Egypt and Sudan address some security dimensions

laws.title: Sisi's Third Presidential Term and Egypt's Debt Crisis
laws.subtitle: Egypt held elections securing Sisi's rule while facing currency collapse and IMF pressures
laws.fullDescription: In December 2023, Egypt held presidential elections in which Abdel Fattah el-Sisi won a third six-year term with 89.6% of the vote in an election that international observers noted lacked genuine competition. Simultaneously, Egypt faced one of its worst economic crises: the Egyptian pound lost over 60% of its value, inflation exceeded 35%, and the country negotiated an expanded $8 billion IMF program requiring devaluation and subsidy cuts. In March 2024, Egypt allowed the pound to float, causing an immediate further crash. The economic stress coincided with the Gaza war's regional impact on tourism, Suez Canal revenues (impacted by Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping), and refugee flows.
laws.penalty: Insulting the President: up to 3 years imprisonment under Penal Code Article 179. Anti-government protest without permit: up to 5 years under Protest Law.
exceptions: Journalists with press credentials have limited investigative protections
Foreign diplomats and international organizations retain some freedom to comment on human rights

quiz.q: What economic measure did Egypt take in March 2024 under IMF program conditions?
options: It fixed the pound at 30 EGP per dollar
It allowed the Egyptian pound to float, causing an immediate sharp depreciation
It introduced a new gold-backed currency
It defaulted on all foreign debt obligations
quiz.explanation: Egypt allowed the Egyptian pound to freely float in March 2024 as an IMF condition, causing an immediate further crash after the pound had already lost over 60% of its value in preceding years.

laws.title: Suez Canal Revenue Collapse and Houthi Crisis
laws.subtitle: Yemen's Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping cut Egypt's vital Suez Canal revenues
laws.fullDescription: The Suez Canal, which Egypt nationalized in 1956, generates approximately $10 billion annually — about 2% of Egypt's GDP and its second-largest foreign currency source. Following the Gaza war's outbreak in October 2023, Yemen's Houthi movement began attacking commercial ships in the Red Sea, targeting vessels with Israeli links. Major shipping companies rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope, bypassing the Suez Canal. By early 2024, Suez Canal traffic dropped by over 40%, costing Egypt an estimated $6 billion annually. Egypt launched diplomatic efforts to end the crisis while also accelerating Suez Canal development projects and economic zone investments to maintain revenues.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized transit through Suez Canal: seizure of vessel and fines. Security violations in Canal Zone: criminal prosecution under Egyptian military law.
exceptions: Canal transit fees vary by vessel type — warships of treaty nations have different arrangements
Emergency routing may qualify for reduced fees under SCA (Suez Canal Authority) criteria

quiz.q: By how much did Suez Canal traffic drop in early 2024 due to Houthi Red Sea attacks?
quiz.explanation: Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping caused over 40% drop in Suez Canal traffic as major shipping lines rerouted around Africa's Cape of Good Hope — costing Egypt an estimated $6 billion in annual revenue at peak diversion rates.

laws.title: Egypt's Emergency Law and Media Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Decades of emergency law normalize expanded state security powers
laws.fullDescription: Egypt has operated under emergency law for most of its modern history. Following the 2011 revolution and 2013 military coup, the state expanded its security apparatus dramatically. The 2018 Cybercrime Law criminalizes online content deemed a threat to national security or public order. Journalists and bloggers face prosecution for reporting on government corruption, military affairs, or human rights abuses. Egypt is among the world's top jailers of journalists. Social media accounts with over 5,000 followers are regulated as media outlets requiring registration.
laws.penalty: Cybercrime violations: up to 5 years and EGP 300,000 fine. Spreading false news: up to 2 years. Social media 'accounts that threaten national security': blocking orders plus up to 1 year imprisonment for operators
exceptions: Foreign diplomatic personnel have immunity
Registered foreign press corps have limited protection but are still subject to deportation
Government-controlled media obviously exempt from restrictions
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Ministry of Communications and Information Technology

quiz.q: Under Egypt's cybercrime regulations, which social media accounts are regulated as media outlets?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's cybercrime framework requires social media accounts with more than 5,000 followers to register as media outlets, treating them like news organizations subject to media law regulations.

laws.title: Egypt's IMF Program and Economic Reform Laws
laws.subtitle: Egypt's recurring IMF loans force painful subsidy cuts and currency devaluations
laws.fullDescription: Egypt has been on multiple IMF programs since 2016, driven by persistent balance of payments crises. The 2024 IMF deal worth $8 billion required Egypt to devalue the pound (lost 60% of value in 2024), reduce energy subsidies, raise interest rates to combat 30%+ inflation, and privatize state-owned enterprises. Egypt's Investment Law and Companies Law were reformed to attract foreign direct investment. A new value-added tax replaced the general sales tax. The army-controlled economy — military companies control an estimated 40-60% of GDP — creates unique structural reform challenges.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion under new VAT regime: fines up to 300% of unpaid tax plus imprisonment. Operating unregistered business: fines and closure. Foreign currency speculation: up to 1 year imprisonment. Investment law violations: cancellation of incentives
exceptions: Military-owned enterprises have de facto exemptions from normal privatization requirements
Special economic zones (like Suez Canal Economic Zone) have separate investment rules
International development bank projects have separate disbursement rules

quiz.q: What percentage of Egypt's GDP is estimated to be controlled by army-linked companies?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's military controls an estimated 40-60% of the national economy through army-affiliated companies operating in construction, food, tourism, and other sectors — creating significant structural reform challenges as the IMF pushes for privatization.

laws.title: Egypt's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Dispute
laws.subtitle: Nile water rights conflict between Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia
laws.fullDescription: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) — Africa's largest dam — has created a major diplomatic and potential conflict between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. Egypt and Sudan rely almost entirely on the Nile; Ethiopia's dam reduces downstream flow during filling phases. Egypt considers GERD an existential threat to its water security and has sought international arbitration. Ethiopia began generating electricity from GERD in 2022. The AU-mediated negotiations have repeatedly stalled. Egypt signed defense agreements with Sudan and has made veiled military threats. A binding agreement on filling and operating rules has not been reached.
laws.penalty: Under Egyptian law: individuals who make agreements with foreign countries that harm Egypt's water rights without authorization: prosecution for treason. Ethiopia's domestic law governs GERD construction. International law: no binding mechanism exists to enforce water allocation in the Nile basin
exceptions: Humanitarian water releases during drought may be required under negotiated frameworks
Scientific monitoring data sharing is theoretically ongoing
Diplomatic communications continue despite the impasse
laws.sourceLabel: Egyptian Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation

quiz.q: What does Egypt consider existential about the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam?
options: Loss of tourism from reduced Nile scenery
Reduced downstream flow threatening Egypt's almost total dependence on the Nile for water
Seismic risk from the dam's weight
quiz.explanation: Egypt considers GERD an existential threat because Egypt depends on the Nile for approximately 97% of its water supply — any significant reduction in downstream flow due to dam filling and operation directly threatens the water security of 100+ million Egyptians.

laws.title: Supreme State Security Prosecution and Emergency Powers
laws.subtitle: Egypt's permanent state of emergency allows extended detention without charge
laws.fullDescription: Egypt operated under a continuous state of emergency from 2017 to 2021 and retains broad emergency-style powers through the Supreme State Security Prosecution (SSSP). The SSSP can detain suspects for extended periods without criminal charges. Persons accused of terrorism or threatening national security can be held for up to 2 years during investigation. The terrorism law (Law 94/2015) broadly defines terrorist acts to include disrupting public order or harming national unity. Bloggers, journalists, and ordinary social media users have been detained under these laws. The Emergency State Security Courts handle cases without normal appeal rights.
laws.penalty: Terrorism charges: 10 years to life imprisonment; joining terrorist organization: 5–25 years; spreading false news about state: up to 5 years
exceptions: Diplomatic immunity for foreign missions
Foreign journalists with properly issued press credentials (limited protection)

quiz.q: How long can Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution hold suspects without charges?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution can detain persons accused of terrorism or national security threats for up to 2 years without criminal charges during the investigation period.

laws.title: Investment Law Reforms and Business Environment Updates
laws.subtitle: Egypt updated investment laws to attract foreign capital amid economic crisis
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's economic crisis — marked by currency devaluation, inflation over 30%, and IMF negotiations — prompted legal reforms to attract foreign investment. The Investment Law 72 of 2017 was updated with new incentives including special economic zones, tax exemptions, and streamlined approval processes. The General Authority for Investment and Free Zones (GAFI) was given enhanced powers to fast-track approvals. Dispute resolution with foreign investors was improved through investment arbitration provisions. However, the real estate investment sector saw foreigners restricted in property purchases in certain areas. The military's extensive economic holdings create parallel informal approval requirements not captured in formal law.
laws.penalty: Violation of investment law conditions: loss of incentives and potential prosecution for misrepresentation; currency regulation violations: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Free Zone companies operate under separate frameworks with different tax treatment
Special category investments (energy, infrastructure) have dedicated legal frameworks

quiz.q: What body has enhanced powers to fast-track foreign investment approvals in Egypt?
options: General Authority for Investment and Free Zones (GAFI)
quiz.explanation: Egypt's General Authority for Investment and Free Zones (GAFI) was given enhanced powers to fast-track investment approvals as part of reforms aimed at attracting foreign capital during Egypt's economic crisis.

laws.title: Gaza Border and Rafah Crossing Legal Status
laws.subtitle: Egypt's management of the Rafah crossing became central to Gaza humanitarian law
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's management of the Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt became critically important during the Gaza conflict. Under various agreements, Egypt has controlled the Palestinian side of Rafah under different arrangements. Egyptian law prohibits unauthorized border crossing and Egypt maintains strict control. During the Gaza conflict, the operational status of Rafah affected hundreds of thousands of people. Egypt faced international pressure to allow more humanitarian aid through. Egyptian law on border management, foreign national entry, and humanitarian corridor operations became subjects of intense international diplomatic and legal discussion. Egypt's national security considerations informed its restrictive approach to the crossing.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized entry into Egypt from Gaza: prosecution under border crossing laws; smuggling through tunnels: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Medical emergencies allowing passage under special coordination
Diplomatic personnel and journalists with special clearances

quiz.q: Why did the Rafah crossing become legally and diplomatically significant during the Gaza conflict?
options: As a key humanitarian aid and civilian evacuation route, its management affected hundreds of thousands under international humanitarian law
quiz.explanation: The Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt became legally and diplomatically significant as virtually the only overland route for humanitarian aid and civilian evacuations during the Gaza conflict, making Egypt's management of the crossing subject to intense international humanitarian law scrutiny.

laws.title: Egypt Cybercrime Law and Social Media Regulation
laws.subtitle: Egypt uses cybercrime laws to restrict online dissent
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Cybercrime Law (Law No. 175 of 2018) criminalizes a wide range of online activities including using the internet to threaten national security, violating privacy through unauthorized device access, and running websites that publish content the government deems threatening. Thousands of websites including news outlets, human rights organizations, and VPN services have been blocked. Journalists and activists have been prosecuted under the law for social media posts.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment and fines up to EGP 300,000 for cybercrime violations; up to 10 years for offenses affecting national security
exceptions: Government and official media online activities
Academic cybersecurity research
Content that has been removed within specified timeframe

quiz.q: What types of websites have been widely blocked under Egypt's cybercrime laws?
options: News outlets, human rights organizations, and VPN services
Only commercial sites without Egyptian registration
quiz.explanation: Egypt has blocked thousands of websites including independent news outlets, human rights organizations, and VPN services under the Cybercrime Law and other national security legislation.

laws.title: Egypt President Sisi Third Term and Constitutional Consolidation
laws.subtitle: Egypt's Sisi wins third term extending control
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's December 2023 presidential election resulted in Abdel Fattah el-Sisi winning a third six-year term with 89.6% of the vote in an election without meaningful opposition. The 2019 constitutional amendments had already extended presidential terms to six years and allowed Sisi to run again. Egypt's political space remains heavily restricted, with thousands of political prisoners, tight media control, and restrictions on civil society. The economic situation remains challenging with high inflation and IMF loan dependence.
laws.penalty: Political opposition activity outside narrow permitted channels: prosecution under terrorism and national security laws; media criticism of government: license revocation and criminal charges
exceptions: State-approved media operates freely
Religious institutions function under monitored conditions
Business associations operate with government coordination

quiz.q: What constitutional change in 2019 enabled Sisi to run for a third presidential term in Egypt?
options: Abolition of presidential term limits entirely
Extension of presidential terms to six years and reset of term count
Creation of a new presidency role
quiz.explanation: Egypt's 2019 constitutional amendments extended presidential terms from four to six years and reset the term count, allowing Sisi to run for what was technically a fresh start under the new rules.

laws.title: Egypt Gaza Crisis and Refugee Policy
laws.subtitle: Egypt manages Palestinian refugee concerns during Gaza conflict
laws.fullDescription: During the Gaza conflict, Egypt faced significant pressure regarding Palestinian refugees. Egypt maintained a firm policy against allowing mass movement of Palestinians from Gaza into Sinai, citing concerns about dismantling Palestinian rights to their land, Egyptian national security, and the precedent of depopulation. Egypt also facilitated hostage negotiations through intelligence cooperation. Domestically, Egypt enacted emergency measures to manage the influx of international journalists and humanitarian workers through Rafah.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized border crossing from Gaza: immediate return; security violations at the border: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Humanitarian cases including medical evacuations
Foreign nationals and dual citizens from Gaza
UN and ICRC personnel with specific authorization

quiz.q: What was Egypt's primary reason for refusing to allow mass Palestinian refugee movement into Sinai?
options: Concerns about dismantling Palestinian land rights, national security, and the precedent of depopulation
quiz.explanation: Egypt's policy against accepting mass Palestinian refugee flows was primarily based on concerns that it would undermine Palestinian rights to their own land, create national security risks in Sinai, and set a precedent of Palestinian depopulation.

laws.title: Cybercrime and Internet Regulation Laws
laws.subtitle: Egypt's framework for monitoring and restricting online activity
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's cybercrime law and associated regulations give authorities broad powers to block websites, monitor online communications, and prosecute online speech. The National Telecom Regulatory Authority (NTRA) can block websites deemed threatening to national security or social peace without court order. Egypt has blocked thousands of websites including news portals, VPN services, and human rights organization sites. Social media users have been prosecuted for posts criticizing the government or military. Encrypted communications apps have faced restrictions.
laws.penalty: Publishing content threatening national security or inciting violence online carries 2 to 5 years imprisonment; operating blocked services carries fines up to EGP 1 million
exceptions: Government communications and official state media exempt
Academic cybersecurity research with institutional approval permitted
International news organizations with Egyptian operating licenses have some protection

quiz.q: Who can order website blocking in Egypt without requiring a court order?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's NTRA (National Telecom Regulatory Authority) has the power to block websites it deems threatening to national security or social peace without needing a prior court order.

laws.title: Investment Law and Special Economic Zones
laws.subtitle: Egypt's framework for attracting foreign investment through SEZs
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted a comprehensive Investment Law and expanded its network of Special Economic Zones to attract foreign investment and create jobs. The law offers foreign investors tax holidays, customs duty exemptions, guarantees against nationalization, simplified dispute resolution through international arbitration, and one-stop-shop licensing through the General Authority for Investment (GAFI). Special zones including Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZone) offer enhanced benefits. Egypt has used investment law reforms to attract Gulf capital especially from Saudi Arabia and UAE following its IMF-backed economic reform program.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent investment registration carries criminal liability; failure to meet investment commitments within agreed timeframes triggers benefit revocation; illegal capital flight from SEZ operations carries fines
exceptions: Micro and small enterprises have simplified investment registration
Non-profit social enterprises have modified investment law treatment
Tourism investments have separate incentive framework through Tourism Development Authority

quiz.q: What major economic zone has Egypt developed around the Suez Canal to attract investment?
quiz.explanation: Egypt developed the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZone) as a major special economic zone leveraging the strategic location of the Suez Canal to attract shipping, manufacturing, and logistics investment with enhanced incentives beyond standard investment law.

laws.title: New Administrative Capital Laws
laws.subtitle: Egypt's legal framework for the new capital city
laws.fullDescription: Egypt has been building a new administrative capital east of Cairo, relocating government ministries and institutions. Special laws established the Administrative Capital for Urban Development (ACUD) company as the developer, set investment rules and property ownership rights in the new capital, created a special administrative authority, and authorized the transfer of government functions and assets. The new capital has been built with Chinese construction and financing. Egypt's new capital reflects President el-Sisi's ambition to create a world-class modern city away from congested Cairo.
laws.penalty: Construction in the new capital without ACUD authorization carries demolition orders; property fraud in new capital developments carries enhanced criminal penalties; squatting in new capital territory carries immediate eviction
exceptions: Diplomatic missions building embassies in the new capital follow diplomatic protocol
Existing communities whose land was acquired have relocation and compensation rights
Construction workers' temporary accommodation camps follow simplified building rules
laws.sourceLabel: Administrative Capital for Urban Development Egypt

quiz.q: Who has been the primary constructor and financier of Egypt's new administrative capital?
options: Saudi Arabia through sovereign wealth funds
China through construction companies and financing
quiz.explanation: China has been the primary partner in building Egypt's new administrative capital, with Chinese state construction companies (particularly China State Construction Engineering Corporation) doing the major construction work financed through Chinese lending arrangements.

laws.title: Egypt IMF Program and Currency Float
laws.subtitle: $8 billion IMF agreement and pound devaluation of 40%
laws.fullDescription: Egypt secured an expanded $8 billion IMF agreement in March 2024, simultaneously floating the Egyptian pound and allowing it to lose approximately 40% of its value against the dollar. The devaluation followed years of maintaining an artificially strong exchange rate that drained foreign currency reserves. Egypt also received a $5 billion package from the UAE's Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, a $1 billion World Bank commitment, and EU development financing. The reforms addressed Egypt's severe foreign currency shortage but caused import prices to spike.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized foreign currency trading outside licensed exchanges: fines of EGP 10,000–50,000 and up to 3 years imprisonment under the Central Bank Law.
exceptions: Tourism industry operators allowed to set USD prices directly for foreign tourists
Export companies retained foreign currency earnings accounts with modified repatriation requirements

quiz.q: Approximately how much did the Egyptian pound lose in value when it was floated in March 2024?
quiz.explanation: The Egyptian pound lost approximately 40% of its value against the US dollar when Egypt floated its currency in March 2024 as part of an $8 billion IMF agreement, ending years of an artificially maintained exchange rate.

laws.title: Egypt Gaza War Role and Rafah Crossing Crisis
laws.subtitle: Cairo's mediation role and humanitarian corridor management
laws.fullDescription: Egypt played a critical role in the Gaza war that began October 7, 2023, serving as the primary mediator in ceasefire negotiations alongside Qatar and the United States. The Rafah crossing between Egypt and Gaza was central to humanitarian aid delivery; Egypt maintained it largely closed except for limited aid convoys, citing security concerns and Israeli pressure. Egypt publicly warned against any forced displacement of Palestinians into Sinai, seeing this as a strategic threat. Egypt and Israel had tensions over the Philadelphi corridor military operations.
laws.penalty: Egypt's national security laws criminalize advocacy for displacing Palestinians into Egyptian territory as threatening national security. Egyptian officials who reveal mediation discussions face prosecution under state secrets laws.
exceptions: Medical evacuations from Gaza through Rafah subject to case-by-case authorizations from Egyptian military
Journalists accompanying official delegations may access restricted border zones under Egyptian press credentials

quiz.q: Which countries were the primary mediators in the Gaza ceasefire negotiations?
options: Egypt, Qatar, and the United States
quiz.explanation: Egypt, Qatar, and the United States served as the primary mediators in Gaza ceasefire negotiations, with Cairo and Doha as key interlocutors given their relationships with both Israel and Hamas. Egypt also played a critical role managing the Rafah crossing for humanitarian aid.

laws.title: Egypt Sisi Third Term and Constitutional Amendments
laws.subtitle: Re-election consolidates extended presidential authority
laws.fullDescription: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi won a third six-year term in December 2023 elections with over 89% of the vote — an election where credible opposition candidates faced obstacles to registration. The 2019 constitutional amendments had extended presidential terms from 4 to 6 years and allowed Sisi to potentially rule until 2030. Egypt's security forces continued the repression of political opposition, with thousands of political prisoners. The election preceded Egypt's significant role in Gaza ceasefire mediation.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized political activity outside state-approved frameworks: criminal prosecution under Egypt's Political Parties Law and Anti-Terrorism Law, with imprisonment of 1–5 years for organizers.
exceptions: Licensed political parties may operate within legally defined parameters including registration requirements
Religious leaders may speak on social issues within government-approved frameworks without political prosecution

quiz.q: What changes did Egypt's 2019 constitutional amendments make to presidential term length?
options: Established presidential term limits for the first time
Changed to a two-round voting system
quiz.explanation: Egypt's 2019 constitutional amendments extended presidential terms from 4 to 6 years and allowed Sisi to reset his term count, enabling him to potentially rule until 2030. The amendments were approved in a referendum with officially 89% support amid opposition boycotts.

laws.title: New Administrative Capital and Infrastructure Investment Laws
laws.subtitle: Laws governing Egypt's new capital city and major development projects
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted legislation governing the New Administrative Capital (NAC), including a special authority with independent regulatory powers, tax incentives for companies relocating, foreign ownership allowances in NAC properties (up to 100%), and simplified business registration. The capital project — costing over $58 billion — was partly financed through property sales to Gulf sovereign wealth funds.
laws.penalty: Unauthorised construction in NAC zone: demolition and fines up to EGP 1 million; property fraud in NAC: up to 10 years imprisonment
exceptions: Government ministries relocating receive facilitated transfer procedures
Diplomatic missions retain ability to maintain Cairo headquarters during transition

quiz.q: What foreign ownership percentage is allowed for properties in Egypt's New Administrative Capital?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's New Administrative Capital legislation allows foreign ownership of up to 100% of properties in the NAC zone, a significant liberalisation designed to attract Gulf and international investment.

laws.title: Egyptian Pound Float and IMF Deal Implementation
laws.subtitle: Egypt devalues currency and secures expanded IMF programme
laws.fullDescription: Egypt allowed the Egyptian pound to depreciate sharply as part of an expanded $8 billion IMF programme, accepting exchange rate flexibility after years of defending an overvalued peg. Fuel subsidies were reduced, electricity tariffs increased, and state asset sales began. Military-linked enterprises were encouraged to exit sectors where they competed with private business.
laws.penalty: Black market forex trading: criminal prosecution; banks violating Central Bank forex circulars: licence review
exceptions: Strategic imports (wheat, medicine) receive preferential forex allocation
Export processing zone companies can maintain foreign currency accounts

quiz.q: How much was Egypt's expanded IMF programme worth?
quiz.explanation: Egypt secured an expanded $8 billion IMF programme in 2024, requiring currency devaluation, subsidy reduction, and privatisation of state assets as conditions for the support package.

laws.title: Benban Solar Park Expansion and Green Corridor
laws.subtitle: Egypt expands world's largest solar complex and plans for export
laws.fullDescription: Egypt expanded the Benban Solar Park — already one of the world's largest concentrated solar facilities in the Western Desert — and enacted legislation enabling a Green Energy Corridor for electricity exports to Europe via submarine cables. The law created a Renewable Energy Investment Zone, offering foreign investors 25-year licences with guaranteed grid connection.
laws.penalty: Solar project developers failing to meet construction milestones: licence penalties and connection delays
exceptions: Small community solar projects in remote desert areas receive simplified permitting
Research facilities testing new solar technologies exempt from commercial production requirements

quiz.q: What is the name of Egypt's massive solar complex in the Western Desert?
quiz.explanation: Benban Solar Park, located in Upper Egypt's Western Desert, is one of the world's largest solar installations — a key pillar of Egypt's renewable energy strategy and its ambitions to export green electricity to Europe.

laws.title: New Administrative Capital and Egyptian Economic Zones Law
laws.subtitle: Mega-project zones with special regulatory regimes
laws.fullDescription: Egypt's Special Economic Zones Law 2025 consolidated regulations for the New Administrative Capital, Ras El-Hekma development zone, and Suez Canal Economic Zone under a unified framework. The law grants zone authorities power to issue single-window permits replacing 26 separate government approvals, provides 10-year corporate tax holidays for qualifying investments, and allows 100% foreign ownership without local partnership requirements. Labour law modifications within zones permit fixed-term contracts without conversion to permanent employment, raising worker advocacy concerns.
laws.penalty: Operating without zone authority permit: project shutdown plus EGP 10 million fine; false investment value declaration: blacklisting from Egyptian government contracts for 5 years; labour violation: EGP 500,000 per affected worker
exceptions: Micro-enterprises (under EGP 1 million capital) may use simplified registration
Strategic investments above $500 million receive individual negotiated terms
Companies in technology sector receive extended 15-year tax holiday

quiz.q: How many separate government approvals does Egypt's Special Economic Zones single-window permit system replace?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's Special Economic Zones Law grants zone authorities power to issue single-window permits that replace 26 separate government approvals, dramatically streamlining investment procedures.

laws.title: Egypt Renewable Energy Export and Suez Green Corridor Act
laws.subtitle: Harnessing desert sun for Europe-bound green energy
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted the Renewable Energy Export and Suez Green Energy Corridor Act 2025, targeting development of the world's largest solar and wind energy export project. The law establishes the Egyptian Renewable Energy Export Authority, authorizes development of 100GW of renewable capacity in the Sinai Peninsula and Western Desert by 2035 for domestic use and European export via high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables, creates green hydrogen production zones along the Gulf of Suez, establishes a 25-year feed-in tariff framework for export projects, and introduces streamlined permitting giving the Egyptian Electricity Authority joint approval powers reducing 12 separate permits to one integrated license. The 'Suez Green Corridor' aims to make Egypt a renewable energy bridge between Africa and Europe.
laws.penalty: Renewable export project without HVDC route approval: EGP 500 million plus shutdown; green hydrogen misclassification: EGP 1 billion; land acquisition for projects without community compensation: project cancellation
exceptions: Domestic renewable projects under 10MW follow simplified residential and commercial framework
Research installations exempt from export corridor requirements
Desert land below productivity threshold may be used for solar without agricultural compensation
laws.sourceLabel: Egypt Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy

quiz.q: What infrastructure will physically connect Egypt's desert renewable energy to European markets under the Suez Green Corridor Act?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's Suez Green Corridor Act plans to connect desert solar and wind energy to European markets via high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables — the most efficient technology for transmitting large amounts of electricity over long distances.

laws.title: Egypt IMF Programme and Political Economy Stabilization
laws.subtitle: Third IMF bailout and economic liberalization
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted the Economic Stabilization and IMF Programme Compliance Act 2025, codifying the structural reforms required under Egypt's third IMF programme. The law mandates phased reduction of energy subsidies with targeted social protection mechanisms, establishes the State Ownership Policy Committee to privatize state-owned enterprises in competitive sectors, creates the Egyptian Investment and Economic Zones Authority consolidating nine separate investment agencies into one, introduces exchange rate flexibility provisions preventing artificial pound management, establishes the Egypt Sovereign Wealth Fund as manager of privatization proceeds, and creates the Digital Customs and Tax Compliance System targeting Egypt's large informal economy. Egypt's economic vulnerabilities — high debt, subsidies, military economic dominance — required sustained reform.
laws.penalty: State enterprise privatization fraud: EGP 2 billion plus criminal prosecution; exchange rate artificial fixing: Central Bank regulatory action; customs evasion: EGP 500 million plus 15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Military-owned enterprises in strategic defence sectors exempt from privatization mandate
Essential medicines and bread subsidies maintained under social protection framework
Small informal traders have 3-year transition to formal compliance

quiz.q: Which Egyptian institution manages the proceeds from the privatization of state-owned enterprises under the 2025 Stabilization Act?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's Economic Stabilization Act establishes the Egypt Sovereign Wealth Fund as the manager of privatization proceeds from selling stakes in state-owned enterprises — a mechanism to ensure revenues from asset sales are managed transparently rather than being absorbed into general government spending.

laws.title: El-Sisi Third Term and Economic Crisis Management Act
laws.subtitle: Currency devaluation, IMF bailout, and political consolidation
laws.fullDescription: President el-Sisi's government, following his third-term election amid mass arrests of opposition figures, enacted legislation to implement Egypt's IMF bailout conditions. The law floats the Egyptian pound (resulting in dramatic devaluation), reduces energy subsidies, and privatizes state assets. It simultaneously expands emergency law provisions, restricts civil society organizations' foreign funding, and broadens terrorism definitions used to imprison journalists and activists.
laws.penalty: Spreading 'false news' about the economy or security situation carries up to five years imprisonment. Unauthorized receipt of foreign funding by NGOs carries up to life imprisonment in severe cases. Participating in unauthorized protests carries up to three years.
exceptions: Foreign-invested companies in special economic zones retain currency repatriation rights even during exchange controls
Journalists from accredited international outlets retain limited reporting protections compared to Egyptian nationals

quiz.q: What economic measure did Egypt implement as part of its IMF bailout conditions?
options: Floating the Egyptian pound, causing dramatic devaluation
Imposing a 50% tariff on all imports
quiz.explanation: Egypt floated the Egyptian pound as part of IMF bailout conditions, resulting in dramatic currency devaluation that significantly increased the cost of living for ordinary Egyptians.

laws.title: Currency Stabilization and Foreign Investment Recovery Act
laws.subtitle: Post-devaluation economic reconstruction
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted economic recovery legislation following multiple pound devaluations and the IMF bailout. The law creates a foreign investment facilitation office with streamlined approvals, reduces state company monopolies in strategic sectors to attract private capital, establishes new sovereign wealth fund investment rules, and implements agricultural subsidy reforms replacing universal bread subsidies with targeted cash transfers to the poorest households.
laws.penalty: Currency speculators who manipulate the newly floated exchange rate face up to 10 years imprisonment. Customs fraud affecting foreign investment facilitation carries up to seven years.
exceptions: Wheat imports for the national bread program retain government price controls regardless of market liberalization
Special economic zone investors in Suez Canal corridor projects receive five-year currency repatriation guarantees

quiz.q: What traditional Egyptian food subsidy did the recovery legislation reform from universal to targeted?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's universal bread (baladi) subsidy, which provided cheap bread to all Egyptians regardless of income, was replaced with targeted cash transfers to the poorest households as a condition of IMF support and fiscal reform.

laws.title: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Water Rights and Nile Diplomacy Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting Egypt's Nile water share from GERD
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted legislation asserting its rights to the Nile's waters amid the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) dispute. The law formalizes Egypt's position that it will not accept any reduction in its 55.5 billion cubic meters annual Nile allocation guaranteed by the 1959 treaty, authorizes the government to pursue all diplomatic and legal options to protect water rights, and creates emergency water rationing protocols for drought scenarios caused by upstream damming.
laws.penalty: This legislation primarily establishes diplomatic and policy frameworks. Egyptian citizens who waste water during declared water conservation emergencies face escalating fines.
exceptions: Humanitarian water allocations for drinking and basic sanitation retain priority during any shortage scenario
Egyptian agricultural users in new land reclamation projects receive different water allocation frameworks than traditional Nile valley farmers

quiz.q: How much water annually does Egypt claim as its guaranteed Nile allocation under the 1959 treaty?
quiz.explanation: Egypt claims 55.5 billion cubic meters of Nile water annually under the 1959 bilateral treaty with Sudan. Ethiopia, which is building GERD, was not a party to that treaty and does not recognize it as binding — creating a fundamental legal dispute.

laws.title: Benban Solar Complex and Green Energy Export Act
laws.subtitle: Egypt as Middle East renewable energy hub
laws.fullDescription: Egypt enacted legislation building on its Benban solar complex — one of the world's largest solar parks — to position Egypt as a regional renewable energy exporter. The law creates a green electricity export framework to Europe via undersea cables, establishes a green hydrogen production program, creates incentives for European energy companies to invest in Egyptian solar and wind projects, and establishes a regulatory framework for the developing Sumed pipeline alternative using green energy.
laws.penalty: Green energy certification fraud carries up to seven years imprisonment. Energy export contracts that misrepresent the renewable sourcing of electricity face contract penalties.
exceptions: Emergency electricity exports during European grid crises may proceed outside standard certification requirements
Research partnerships between Egyptian and European universities on renewable technology retain simplified approvals

quiz.q: What is remarkable about Egypt's Benban Solar Complex near Aswan?
options: It is one of the world's largest solar parks
It uses only desert sand for cooling
It was built by Egyptian engineers alone without foreign assistance
quiz.explanation: The Benban Solar Complex in Upper Egypt's Aswan governorate is one of the world's largest solar energy facilities, with capacity of approximately 1.8 gigawatts from over 30 individual solar parks. It takes advantage of Egypt's exceptional solar irradiation in the Sahara.

laws.title: Egypt IMF Extended Fund Facility and Economic Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Currency Devaluation and Fiscal Consolidation Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements Egypt's expanded IMF program following currency crises and foreign exchange shortage. The law allows the Egyptian pound to float freely, eliminates import restrictions that had caused shortages, establishes the privatization program for state enterprises, reduces energy subsidies, creates a social protection expansion for vulnerable populations, and establishes an independent central bank oversight board.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for currency manipulation; fines for businesses violating foreign exchange regulations
exceptions: Essential medicines exempt from import restriction reforms
Social protection spending has protected floor regardless of fiscal adjustment

quiz.q: What does Egypt's IMF Reform Act allow the Egyptian pound to do?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's IMF Reform Act allows the Egyptian pound to float freely, ending artificial currency controls that caused foreign exchange shortages.

laws.title: Egypt Sinai Border Security and Gaza Civilian Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Israel-Gaza Conflict Buffer Zone and Refugee Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes Egypt's legal framework for managing the Gaza border during and after the Israel-Hamas conflict. The law creates security protocols for the Rafah crossing, establishes humanitarian assistance corridors, maintains Egypt's firm position against accepting Palestinian refugees in Sinai (which Egypt views as a threat to Palestinian statehood), creates reconstruction involvement frameworks, and establishes mediation frameworks.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for illegal border crossing from Gaza; security enforcement for Sinai buffer zone violations
exceptions: Medical emergency evacuations from Gaza have special humanitarian status
International humanitarian organization workers have access credentials

quiz.q: What is Egypt's official position on accepting Palestinian refugees in Sinai?
quiz.explanation: Egypt firmly opposes accepting Palestinian refugees in Sinai, viewing it as a threat to Palestinian aspirations for statehood in Gaza and the West Bank.

laws.title: Egypt New Administrative Capital and Decentralization Act
laws.subtitle: Capital City Transfer and Urban Development Law
laws.fullDescription: Governs the phased transfer of Egypt's government to the New Administrative Capital east of Cairo. The law establishes the legal capital status of the New Administrative Capital, creates decentralization mechanisms for Cairo governorate, establishes the New Urban Communities Authority's expanded role, creates investment frameworks for the new city, and manages the transition of ministries and the presidential palace.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for government bodies failing to meet relocation timelines
exceptions: Parliament retains Cairo presence during extended session periods
Emergency operations may be conducted from Cairo during transition

quiz.q: Where is Egypt's New Administrative Capital located relative to Cairo?
quiz.explanation: Egypt's New Administrative Capital is located east of Cairo in the desert, designed to relieve Cairo's overcrowding and modernize government operations.

laws.title: IMF Bailout and Currency Devaluation Program
laws.subtitle: Egypt's Economic Stabilization Amid Debt Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Egypt secured a significantly expanded IMF program worth over $8 billion in 2024, accompanied by substantial Egyptian pound devaluation and subsidy cuts. The program aimed to address chronic foreign currency shortages and unsustainable debt levels. Social tensions rose as inflation affected food and energy prices.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; social and economic hardship from austerity
exceptions: Social protection programs for lowest income brackets
Phased implementation of subsidy reforms

quiz.q: What major economic adjustment did Egypt make as part of its IMF program?
quiz.explanation: Egypt devalued its pound significantly as part of its IMF program conditions, which helped address foreign currency shortages but increased inflation.

laws.title: El-Sisi Third Term and Constitutional Changes
laws.subtitle: Egypt Extends Presidential Terms to Six Years
laws.fullDescription: President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi won a third presidential term in December 2023 elections widely considered uncompetitive. Constitutional changes had extended presidential terms from four to six years, allowing Sisi potentially to rule until 2030. Egypt continued facing economic crisis, political repression, and concerns over the Gaza war's impact on tourism and Rafah border crossings.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for political opposition; emergency law provisions
exceptions: Limited opposition party activities permitted
Constitutional court nominal independence

quiz.q: How long are presidential terms in Egypt after the constitutional amendment?
quiz.explanation: Egypt extended presidential terms from four to six years through constitutional amendment, allowing Sisi potentially to rule until 2030 after his third term victory.

laws.title: Desalination and Renewable Energy Expansion
laws.subtitle: Egypt Addresses Water Scarcity and Power Deficit
laws.fullDescription: Egypt embarked on a major desalination and renewable energy expansion program to address water scarcity and chronic electricity shortages. The government partnered with UAE-based companies and others for large-scale solar and wind projects. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam continued creating tensions over Nile water allocation.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; energy regulatory compliance
exceptions: Subsidy reform phasing
Nile water rights treaty framework

quiz.q: What ongoing dispute affects Egypt's Nile water supply planning?
options: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam reducing downstream flow
quiz.explanation: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam reduces Nile water flow downstream to Egypt, creating an ongoing dispute that complicates Egypt's water supply planning.

laws.title: New Administrative Capital and Infrastructure Push
